## Discipline 19 — Latency Budget Allocation Across Platforms

**Sources:** https://arxiv.org/html/2603.23640 | https://johannesgaessler.github.io/llamacpp_performance | https://openbenchmarking.org/test/pts/llama-cpp | https://mlcommons.org/2025/09/small-llm-inference-5-1/ | https://bentoml.com/llm/inference-optimization/llm-inference-metrics | https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/time-to-first-token-ttft | https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/benchmarking/llm/latest/metrics.html

**What the open floor shows:**

Latency budget is the total wall-clock time a user or orchestrator is willing to wait for a kernel to return a result. How that budget is allocated differs fundamentally between the three deployment tiers.

**Verified latency breakdown (8 GB floor, conservative figures from open benchmarks):**

|Platform tier |Dominant latency source |Observed token/s range (open benchmarks)|Sustainable sustained rate |Notes |
|---------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|Mobile (8 GB, passive cooling) |Thermal throttling within 2–6 inference runs|10–40 tok/s peak, 6–22 tok/s sustained |~6–12 tok/s after throttle onset |arxiv.org/html/2603.23640: 44% degradation within 2 inferences; hard OS-enforced floor at iteration 6 on some Android hardware|
|Desktop/PC (active cooling, wall power)|Memory bandwidth |14–61 tok/s (7B–9B Q4 models) |Sustained at near-peak for minutes|johannesgaessler.github.io/llamacpp_performance; openbenchmarking.org/test/pts/llama-cpp |
|Cloud (GPU-accelerated instance) |Network RTT + cold start |100–500+ tok/s |Sustained at high rate |Varies by instance class; TTFT dominated by network |

**Verified latency allocation rules:**

- **Mobile local-only budget:** For interactive use, allocate ≤3 seconds TTFT as the user-experience threshold. With llama.cpp on 8 GB mobile hardware running a Q4 3B–7B model, cold-start (model load from storage) is the dominant cost at 2–8 seconds; subsequent tokens at 6–22 tok/s. Budget planning must account for the cold-start separately from generation latency.
- **Desktop hybrid budget:** TTFT is dominated by model load and KV cache warmup. With mmap() support in llama.cpp, model weights load at near-instant on warm systems. Generation at 14–61 tok/s is sustainable without throttle for the duration of typical tasks (minutes, not seconds). Latency budget for desktop is generation-dominated, not thermal-dominated.
- **Cloud full-offload budget:** Network round-trip is the irreducible floor. For tasks requiring large context or long generation, cloud is the appropriate tier. For short tasks (under ~200 tokens), cloud offload may not improve wall-clock time vs. a warmed local model.

**Key design rule:** The 8 GB mobile floor means local inference is viable for 3B–7B Q4 models with careful context limits (–ctx-size 4096 or lower). Exceeding context size causes KV cache bloat that consumes remaining headroom (github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/9784).

-----

### 19-EX — Extended: Latency Budget — Full Decomposition, SLO Design, and Per-Use-Case Allocation Tables

**Sources added:** https://mlcommons.org/2025/09/small-llm-inference-5-1/ | https://bentoml.com/llm/inference-optimization/llm-inference-metrics | https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/time-to-first-token-ttft | https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/benchmarking/llm/latest/metrics.html

#### 19-EX.1 — Full Latency Decomposition Model

Total end-to-end latency (E2EL) for a single inference request has four additive components. Each can be independently measured and optimized.

```
E2EL = T_queue + T_prefill (TTFT component) + T_generate + T_network

Where:
T_queue = time waiting in the request queue before inference starts
(zero for single-user local inference; nonzero under concurrency or rate limiting)
T_prefill = time to process the input prompt and build KV cache
(dominates TTFT; scales with input token count and model size)
T_generate = (output_tokens - 1) × ITL
(ITL = inter-token latency = 1 / token_rate)
T_network = 0 for local; 50–200ms round-trip for cloud (verified: bentoml.com/llm/inference-optimization/llm-inference-metrics)
```

**TTFT specifically** = T_queue + T_prefill (plus T_network if cloud). On a warmed local 7B Q4 model with a 256-token prompt, T_prefill is approximately 0.3–0.5 seconds at 6–22 tok/s sustained mobile rate. Cold-start (T_cold_load) is a separate pre-TTFT cost of 2–8 seconds, not included in TTFT after the model is resident in RAM.

MLPerf Inference 5.1 (mlcommons.org/2025/09/small-llm-inference-5-1/) defines the industry-standard interactive SLO as: **TTFT ≤ 500ms and TPOT ≤ 30ms**. This is a GPU server target. On 8 GB mobile hardware, TTFT ≤ 500ms is achievable only on a warm model with short prompts (≤64 tokens). The realistic interactive target for local 8 GB mobile inference is TTFT ≤ 3s with prompt ≤256 tokens.

#### 19-EX.2 — Per-Use-Case Latency Budget Table

Different kernel task types have different acceptable latency envelopes. The following table maps task type to acceptable E2EL, acceptable TTFT, and the platform tier that can service that task within budget.

|Task type |Max acceptable E2EL|Max acceptable TTFT|Viable on 8 GB mobile?|Viable on desktop?|Notes |
|-------------------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|----------------------|------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|Interactive chat, single turn |5 s |2 s |Yes (warm model) |Yes |Cold start adds 2–8 s; keep model resident |
|Code completion (short, ≤100 tok) |3 s |1 s |Marginal |Yes |Mobile thermal may degrade on 3rd+ call |
|Structured JSON output (small schema)|8 s |3 s |Yes |Yes |Grammar overhead adds ~10–20% ITL (github.com/otriscon/llm-structured-output)|
|Structured output + file write (zip) |30 s |5 s |Yes (single session) |Yes |File I/O cost: negligible vs. generation |
|Long-form generation (≥1000 tok) |120 s |5 s |Risky (thermal) |Yes |Mobile: thermal kill risk after ~6 runs; use cooldown or cloud |
|Tool call + multi-turn agent loop |60 s per cycle |3 s |No (thermal stack) |Yes |Mobile: 3+ back-to-back calls trigger degradation cascade |
|Background batch summarization |No hard limit |No hard limit |Yes (throttled) |Yes |Acceptable at 6–12 tok/s sustained; no user-facing impact |
|Cloud handoff continuation |10 s (for handoff) |N/A |Trigger platform |Cloud |Includes serialization (~500ms) + network RTT + cloud TTFT |

#### 19-EX.3 — Memory Bandwidth as the Binding Desktop Constraint

For desktop CPU inference, token generation rate is bounded by memory bandwidth, not compute (johannesgaessler.github.io/llamacpp_performance). This is verified at the hardware level:

- LLM token generation is memory-bandwidth-bound: each token requires reading all model weights from RAM once. For a 7B Q4 model (~3.8 GB), generating one token requires ~3.8 GB of RAM read at memory bandwidth speed.
- Dual-channel DDR4-3200 provides ~50 GB/s bandwidth → theoretical max ~13 tok/s for a 7B Q4 model on CPU-only inference.
- With GPU acceleration (even integrated), effective bandwidth increases significantly. An RTX 3070Ti at ~448 GB/s VRAM bandwidth → theoretical ~118 tok/s for the same model fully in VRAM.
- Observed benchmarks (johannesgaessler.github.io) confirm token/s scales near-linearly with memory frequency up to the bandwidth saturation point. Adding more CPU threads beyond the number needed to saturate memory bandwidth is detrimental — observed 8→9 thread performance drop on an 8-physical-core system.

**Practical implication for latency budgeting on desktop:** The latency budget for desktop CPU inference is:

```
ITL_desktop_cpu ≈ model_size_gb / (ram_bandwidth_gb_s) seconds per token
```

For 7B Q4 (3.8 GB) on DDR4-3200 dual-channel (≈50 GB/s):

```
ITL ≈ 3.8 / 50 = 0.076 s/token = ~13 tok/s theoretical
```

Observed benchmarks land at 14–20 tok/s for 7B on modern dual-channel desktop CPUs, consistent with this model plus instruction-set optimization overhead.

#### 19-EX.4 — NUMA Interaction with Latency on Multi-Socket Desktop

From the llama.cpp community (github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/11765 and huggingface.co/blog/Doctor-Shotgun/llamacpp-moe-offload-guide):

- Disabling NUMA in BIOS (or via `numactl`) on multi-socket desktop hardware improved token/s from 5 → 8 tok/s on a 14B model in one documented case.
- Cross-socket memory access degrades llama.cpp performance because the model’s weight tensors are accessed sequentially but may be split across NUMA nodes, causing remote memory latency on every token.
- **For 8 GB floor single-socket systems** (all current mobile and most desktop systems in scope), NUMA is not relevant. This becomes relevant only for multi-socket workstations.
- SMT (hyperthreading) is detrimental to inference performance: “Inference does not benefit from SMT, in fact it hurts it” (github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/3167). Set thread count to physical core count only.

#### 19-EX.5 — Latency Measurement Implementation

Standard TTFT and ITL measurement, implemented in Python against any OpenAI-compatible llama.cpp HTTP server endpoint:

```python
import time, requests

def measure_latency(endpoint: str, prompt: str, max_tokens: int = 128) -> dict:
payload = {
"prompt": prompt,
"max_tokens": max_tokens,
"stream": True,
"temperature": 0.0 # deterministic for benchmarking
}

t_request = time.perf_counter()
t_first_token = None
token_timestamps = []

with requests.post(f"{endpoint}/completion", json=payload, stream=True) as resp:
for line in resp.iter_lines():
if line:
t_now = time.perf_counter()
if t_first_token is None:
t_first_token = t_now
token_timestamps.append(t_now)

ttft = t_first_token - t_request
itl_values = [token_timestamps[i] - token_timestamps[i-1]
for i in range(1, len(token_timestamps))]
mean_itl = sum(itl_values) / len(itl_values) if itl_values else 0
e2el = token_timestamps[-1] - t_request if token_timestamps else 0

return {
"ttft_s": round(ttft, 4),
"mean_itl_s": round(mean_itl, 4),
"tok_per_s": round(1 / mean_itl, 1) if mean_itl > 0 else 0,
"e2el_s": round(e2el, 4),
"output_tokens": len(token_timestamps)
}
```

This measurement function follows the NVIDIA NIM benchmarking definition of TTFT (docs.nvidia.com/nim/benchmarking/llm/latest/metrics.html): time from request submission to first token receipt, inclusive of queuing and prefill.

#### 19-EX.6 — Latency Budget Enforcement as a Spawn Trigger

The latency budget table from 19-EX.2 can be used as an automated spawn trigger. If a running kernel’s measured E2EL exceeds the task’s acceptable ceiling, that is an independent signal — separate from thermal or RAM — to spawn the remaining work to a faster platform:

```python
def check_latency_budget(task_type: str, observed_e2el_s: float) -> str:
BUDGETS = {
"interactive_chat": 5.0,
"code_completion": 3.0,
"structured_output": 8.0,
"long_form": 120.0,
"agent_loop": 60.0,
}
budget = BUDGETS.get(task_type, 30.0)
ratio = observed_e2el_s / budget
if ratio > 1.5:
return "SPAWN_CLOUD" # 50% over budget: must offload
if ratio > 1.0:
return "QUEUE" # over budget: queue for next slot
return "LOCAL"
```

## Discipline 20 — Kernel Lifecycle Telemetry Logging Standard

**Sources:** https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2024/llm-observability/ | https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/llm-otel-semantic-convention/ | https://grafana.com/blog/a-complete-guide-to-llm-observability-with-opentelemetry-and-grafana-cloud/ | https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2025/ai-agent-observability/

**What the open floor shows:**

There is now an open standard for LLM telemetry: **OpenTelemetry GenAI Semantic Conventions**, currently at v1.37 (verified at datadoghq.com). This is the factual baseline for a universal kernel lifecycle log format. The convention is provider-agnostic and works equally on mobile, desktop, and cloud.

**Minimum required log fields per kernel lifecycle event (verified against OTel GenAI SemConv):**

```
spawn_time: ISO 8601 timestamp at kernel instantiation
env_fingerprint: {platform_class: "mobile|desktop|cloud", ram_gb: 8, quantization: "Q4_K_M", model_params_b: 7}
telemetry_snapshot: {token_s: float, ram_used_mb: int, ram_headroom_mb: int, thermal_state: "nominal|hot|throttled"}
task_type: "generation|structured_output|tool_call|spawn_child"
input_tokens: int # gen_ai.usage.input_tokens
output_tokens: int # gen_ai.usage.output_tokens
exit_code: "success|oom|thermal_kill|timeout|spawn_handoff"
duration_ms: int
```

**Why these fields specifically:**

- `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens` are defined fields in OTel GenAI SemConv v1.37 (datadoghq.com/blog/llm-otel-semantic-convention/).
- `thermal_state` is not yet a standard OTel field but is empirically necessary: the arxiv thermal study (arxiv.org/html/2603.23640) demonstrates that thermal state is the primary predictor of sustained mobile inference degradation.
- `exit_code: "thermal_kill"` maps to the verified OS-enforced GPU frequency floor termination observed in the mobile thermal benchmark.

**Open tooling for implementation:**

- OpenTelemetry Python SDK: free, Apache 2.0.
- Prometheus + Grafana for metric visualization: free, open source.
- OpenLIT (github.com/openlit): MIT-licensed, OTel-native.

**Implementation pattern (pseudocode):**

```python

from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider

tracer = trace.get_tracer("kernel-lifecycle")

with tracer.start_as_current_span("kernel_spawn") as span:
span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", task_type)
span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", input_tokens)
span.set_attribute("env.ram_headroom_mb", ram_headroom_mb)
span.set_attribute("thermal.state", thermal_state)
# ... run kernel ...
span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", output_tokens)
span.set_attribute("kernel.exit_code", exit_code)
```

#### 20-EX.2 — Telemetry Aggregation: Session-Level Metrics

Individual span logs answer “what happened in this kernel call.” Session-level aggregation answers “how did this session perform overall.” The session-level aggregate is computed at session close:

```python
def compute_session_summary(spans: list[dict]) -> dict:
total_tokens = sum(s["task"]["total_tokens"] for s in spans)
total_time_ms = sum(s["kernel"]["duration_ms"] for s in spans)
thermal_kills = sum(1 for s in spans if s["kernel"]["exit_code"] == "thermal_kill")
spawns = sum(1 for s in spans if s["task"]["spawn_triggered"])
tok_rates = [s["environment"]["token_s_at_spawn"] for s in spans]

return {
"session_tokens_total": total_tokens,
"session_duration_ms": total_time_ms,
"mean_token_s": total_tokens / (total_time_ms / 1000),
"thermal_kills": thermal_kills,
"cloud_spawns": spawns,
"peak_token_s": max(tok_rates),
"final_token_s": tok_rates[-1],
"degradation_over_session": (tok_rates[0] - tok_rates[-1]) / tok_rates[0]
if tok_rates[0] > 0 else 0
}
```

The `degradation_over_session` field directly measures the cumulative thermal impact across the session. A value above 0.40 (40%) is the verified boundary for cloud spawn eligibility (discipline 18).

#### 20-EX.3 — Drift Detection Across Sessions

Session summaries enable cross-session drift detection: identifying when a device’s sustained inference performance is degrading over time due to thermal management policy changes, OS updates, or hardware wear.

```python
def detect_drift(historical_sessions: list[dict], window: int = 10) -> dict:
"""
Compare mean_token_s of the last `window` sessions
against the baseline (first `window` sessions).
Flag if drift exceeds 15%.
"""
if len(historical_sessions) < window * 2:
return {"drift_detected": False, "reason": "insufficient_data"}

baseline = historical_sessions[:window]
recent = historical_sessions[-window:]

baseline_mean = sum(s["mean_token_s"] for s in baseline) / window
recent_mean = sum(s["mean_token_s"] for s in recent) / window

drift_ratio = (baseline_mean - recent_mean) / baseline_mean

return {
"drift_detected": drift_ratio > 0.15,
"drift_ratio": round(drift_ratio, 4),
"baseline_mean_tok_s": round(baseline_mean, 2),
"recent_mean_tok_s": round(recent_mean, 2),
"recommendation": "reduce_context_size" if drift_ratio > 0.15 else "nominal"
}
```

A 15% cross-session drift flag is conservative. The peer-reviewed benchmark (arxiv.org/html/2410.03613v3) documents 10–20% session-to-session degradation in multi-run mobile inference even with warm-up. Sustained drift above 15% across 10+ sessions suggests an environmental change (background process, thermal paste degradation, OS throttle policy change) that warrants investigation.

## Discipline 21 — Mobile 8 GB Edge-Case Handling

**Sources:** https://arxiv.org/html/2603.23640 | https://arxiv.org/html/2410.03613v3 | https://localllm.in/blog/llamacpp-vram-requirements-for-local-llms | https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/9784

**What the open floor shows:**

The 8 GB mobile RAM floor is not a comfortable ceiling — it is a hard constraint requiring active management. Verified failure modes from open research and the llama.cpp community are:

**Failure mode 1: KV cache bloat.** llama.cpp by default allocates a fixed memory block including the full max context size KV cache at initialization. On 8 GB hardware running a 7B Q4 model (~3.8 GB model weights), a default 128K context KV cache can easily exhaust remaining headroom. **Mitigation:** Always set `--ctx-size 4096` or lower (github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/9784). KV cache quantization (`--cache-type-k q8_0`) approximately halves KV cache memory at minimal quality cost.

**Failure mode 2: Thermal throttle cascade.** Mobile hardware degrades 44% throughput within 2 consecutive inference runs. The Android thermal governor can enforce a hard GPU frequency floor, terminating inference entirely. **Mitigation:** Implement cooldown intervals; minimum recommended: allow CPU temperature to return below “nominal” state.

**Failure mode 3: Cold-start latency spike.** First token on a cold model load takes 2–8+ seconds for 7B models on 8 GB mobile hardware. **Mitigation:** Use mmap()-backed model loading; keep model resident via background process.

**Failure mode 4: Multi-LLM concurrent RAM exhaustion.** Running more than one model simultaneously on 8 GB is not viable for 7B class models. Practical limit is one 7B model plus OS overhead, or one 3B plus a smaller companion. **Mitigation:** Single-model time-multiplexed orchestration.

**Expert eviction (SSD fallback):** For MoE models, llama.cpp supports partial layer offload where some layers stream from storage. Viable for background tasks, not interactive generation.

#### 21-EX.2 — KV Cache Budget Calculator

Before starting a session on 8 GB hardware, compute available KV cache budget to determine safe context size:

```python
def compute_safe_ctx_size(
model_size_gb: float, # measured: ~3.8 for 7B Q4, ~2.2 for 3B Q6
ram_total_gb: float = 8.0,
os_overhead_gb: float = 1.5,
safety_buffer_gb: float = 0.4,
kv_bytes_per_token: float = 0.0005 # ~0.5 MB per 1000 tokens for 7B Q4
) -> int:
"""
Returns the safe --ctx-size value for llama.cpp.
kv_bytes_per_token: conservative estimate; varies by model architecture.
For 7B with GQA: typically lower. For older 7B: up to 1 MB per 1000 tokens.
"""
available_for_kv = ram_total_gb - model_size_gb - os_overhead_gb - safety_buffer_gb
if available_for_kv <= 0:
return 512 # absolute floor; model barely fits
max_tokens = int((available_for_kv * 1024) / (kv_bytes_per_token * 1024))
# Round down to nearest power of 2 for llama.cpp alignment
ctx_sizes = [512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192]
safe = max(s for s in ctx_sizes if s <= max_tokens)
return safe

# Example: 7B Q4 on 8 GB
# available_for_kv = 8.0 - 3.8 - 1.5 - 0.4 = 2.3 GB
# max_tokens ≈ 2.3 * 1024 / 0.5 = 4710 tokens → safe ctx = 4096
print(compute_safe_ctx_size(3.8)) # → 4096
```

This confirms the empirical guidance from github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/9784: `--ctx-size 4096` is the practical upper bound for a 7B Q4 model on 8 GB hardware with OS overhead.

#### 21-EX.3 — Thermal Cooldown Timer with Exponential Back-Off

The benchmark data (arxiv.org/html/2603.23640) establishes that a 1-second inter-inference gap is insufficient for thermal recovery. The cooldown required depends on how deep into the thermal envelope the device has gone.

```python
import time

THERMAL_COOLDOWN_TABLE = {
"nominal": 0, # no cooldown needed
"hot": 15, # 15 seconds: allow CPU/GPU frequency to recover
"throttled": 45, # 45 seconds: significant heat buildup; needs real cooldown
"kill": 120, # 2 minutes: hard thermal event; OS may have already enforced pause
}

def thermal_cooldown(current_state: str, verbose: bool = True):
wait = THERMAL_COOLDOWN_TABLE.get(current_state, 0)
if wait > 0:
if verbose:
print(f"[thermal] Cooling down for {wait}s (state: {current_state})")
time.sleep(wait)
return wait

def adaptive_inference_loop(tasks: list, run_inference_fn):
"""
Runs tasks with adaptive thermal cooldown between each.
Uses exponential back-off if thermal state does not improve.
"""
thermal_state = "nominal"
cooldown_multiplier = 1.0

for task in tasks:
if thermal_state != "nominal":
actual_wait = thermal_cooldown(thermal_state) * cooldown_multiplier
# Re-check thermal after cooldown
thermal_state = read_thermal_state()
if thermal_state != "nominal":
cooldown_multiplier = min(cooldown_multiplier * 2, 8.0) # cap at 8×
else:
cooldown_multiplier = 1.0 # reset on recovery

result = run_inference_fn(task)
thermal_state = read_thermal_state()

return results
```

#### 21-EX.4 — Thread Count Optimization for Mobile

From arxiv.org/html/2410.03613v1: “Setting the number of threads equal to the number of big cores (prime and performance cores) achieves optimal performance. Adding efficiency cores may degrade performance.”

This is the llama.cpp `--threads` parameter. On a typical modern phone SoC with a big.LITTLE architecture (e.g., 1 prime + 3 performance + 4 efficiency cores), the optimal thread count is 4 (prime + performance cores only). Setting threads to 8 (all cores) routes inference work to efficiency cores that have lower memory bandwidth, causing a net slowdown.

```python
import subprocess

def get_optimal_thread_count() -> int:
"""
Read CPU topology from /sys/devices/system/cpu/
and return count of big/performance cores only.
On Linux/Android (Termux-accessible).
"""
try:
# Read max frequencies per CPU
import os
freqs = {}
cpu_base = "/sys/devices/system/cpu"
for cpu in os.listdir(cpu_base):
if cpu.startswith("cpu") and cpu[3:].isdigit():
freq_path = f"{cpu_base}/{cpu}/cpufreq/cpuinfo_max_freq"
if os.path.exists(freq_path):
with open(freq_path) as f:
freqs[cpu] = int(f.read().strip())
if not freqs:
return 4 # safe default
max_freq = max(freqs.values())
threshold = max_freq * 0.7 # big cores are ≥70% of max
big_cores = sum(1 for f in freqs.values() if f >= threshold)
return max(1, big_cores)
except Exception:
return 4 # safe default
```

#### 21-EX.5 — Multi-Failure Combination Handling

The most dangerous scenario is when multiple failure modes trigger simultaneously (KV cache near-full + thermal hot + RAM headroom tight). A priority-ordered response:

```python
def handle_multi_failure(state: dict) -> str:
"""
Returns one of: "reduce_context", "cooldown", "spawn_cloud", "deny_all"
Priority: safety first (OOM/thermal kill), then performance, then context.
"""
if state["thermal"] == "kill" or state["ram_headroom_mb"] < 200:
return "deny_all" # hardware at limit: stop everything

if state["thermal"] == "throttled" and state["ram_headroom_mb"] < 400:
return "spawn_cloud" # both thermal + RAM: must offload

if state["thermal"] in ("hot", "throttled"):
return "cooldown" # thermal dominant: wait first

if state["ram_headroom_mb"] < 400:
return "reduce_context" # RAM dominant: shrink context

return "continue"
```

### 22-EX — Extended: Parity Checklist — Automated Runner, Variance Tolerance Table, Known Parity Gaps, and Cross-Platform Regression Suite

**Sources added:** https://openbenchmarking.org/test/pts/llama-cpp | https://llm-tracker.info/howto/LLM-Inference-Benchmarking-Cheat%E2%80%91Sheet-for-Hardware-Reviewers | https://arxiv.org/html/2410.03613v3

#### 22-EX.1 — Automated Parity Checker (Python)

```python
import subprocess, hashlib, json, time

class PlatformParityChecker:
"""
Runs the 20-point parity checklist against a live llama.cpp server endpoint.
"""

def __init__(self, endpoint: str, model_path: str, ctx_size: int = 4096):
self.endpoint = endpoint
self.model_path = model_path
self.ctx_size = ctx_size
self.results = {}

def check_01_model_hash(self) -> bool:
"""Check 1: Same GGUF file (SHA-256 hash match)."""
sha = hashlib.sha256()
with open(self.model_path, "rb") as f:
for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(8192), b""):
sha.update(chunk)
self.results["model_hash"] = sha.hexdigest()
return True # caller compares across platforms

def check_06_warmup_token_rate(self) -> dict:
"""Check 6: Measure token/s after warmup run (not cold start)."""
# Run one warmup pass
self._run_inference("warmup prompt", max_tokens=32)
# Measure on second pass
t0 = time.perf_counter()
result = self._run_inference("benchmark prompt " * 10, max_tokens=128)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
tok_s = result["output_tokens"] / elapsed
self.results["tok_s_warm"] = round(tok_s, 2)
return {"tok_s": tok_s, "pass": tok_s > 2.0} # floor: 2 tok/s on any platform

def check_08_thread_count(self) -> dict:
"""Check 8: Verify thread count = physical performance core count."""
# Read from /proc/cpuinfo or llama.cpp server info endpoint
import requests
info = requests.get(f"{self.endpoint}/props").json()
threads_set = info.get("n_threads", -1)
self.results["threads"] = threads_set
return {"threads": threads_set, "pass": threads_set > 0}

def check_09_memory_footprint(self) -> dict:
"""Check 9: Total memory below 8 GB."""
import psutil
used = psutil.virtual_memory().used / (1024**3)
self.results["ram_used_gb"] = round(used, 2)
return {"ram_used_gb": used, "pass": used < 8.0}

def check_20_sustained_degradation(self) -> dict:
"""Check 20: Run 5 consecutive inferences; final tok/s ≥ 50% of first."""
rates = []
for i in range(5):
t0 = time.perf_counter()
result = self._run_inference("test prompt " * 20, max_tokens=64)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
rates.append(result["output_tokens"] / elapsed)
time.sleep(0.5) # minimal gap
ratio = rates[-1] / rates[0] if rates[0] > 0 else 0
self.results["degradation_ratio_5runs"] = round(1 - ratio, 4)
return {"rates": [round(r,2) for r in rates],
"final_ratio": round(ratio, 4),
"pass": ratio >= 0.50}

def run_all(self) -> dict:
checks = [
self.check_01_model_hash,
self.check_06_warmup_token_rate,
self.check_08_thread_count,
self.check_09_memory_footprint,
self.check_20_sustained_degradation,
]
passed = sum(1 for c in checks if c().get("pass", False))
return {"passed": passed, "total": len(checks), "details": self.results}
```

#### 22-EX.2 — Variance Tolerance Table

Identical inputs on different platforms will not produce bit-for-bit identical outputs due to floating-point non-determinism across hardware backends (CPU AVX2 vs. CPU NEON vs. GPU CUDA). Acceptable variance ranges:

|Metric |Acceptable variance|Fail condition|Notes |
|------------------------------------------|-------------------|--------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|Output token count (deterministic, temp=0)|0% |Any difference|At temperature=0, output must be identical across platforms for same model/quantization |
|Output token count (stochastic, temp>0) |±15% |>30% |Stochastic variance is expected; extreme divergence suggests sampling mismatch |
|TTFT (warm model) |±50% |>3× |Platform differences in memory bandwidth cause TTFT variation; 3× is excessive |
|Sustained tok/s |±40% |>60% |Mobile vs. desktop will differ; 60% divergence suggests misconfiguration |
|Memory footprint (same model + ctx) |±5% |>15% |llama.cpp uses fixed block allocation; large variance = different ctx-size or quantization|
|Exit code |0% |Any difference|“success” must be the exit code across all platforms for the same task |

#### 22-EX.3 — Known Parity Gaps (Not Bugs — By Design)

These are verified cross-platform behavioral differences that are not failures:

1. **Thread count differs across platforms.** Correct: optimal thread count is hardware-specific (big cores only on mobile; all cores on desktop with hyperthreading disabled).
1. **Cold-start TTFT differs by 2–8 seconds.** Correct: storage I/O speed differs. Parity is only expected on warm model.
1. **Flash attention availability differs.** `-fa 1` is supported on some backends but not all. Where unavailable, the runtime silently falls back; token output is identical, TTFT may differ.
1. **GPU offload (`--n-gpu-layers`) differs.** Mobile may have no GPU backend; desktop may have full GPU offload. Set `--n-gpu-layers 0` for CPU-parity testing; allow GPU offload for performance testing.
1. **Context memory layout differs by OS page size.** Linux uses 4KB pages; some mobile kernels use 16KB. llama.cpp handles this internally; no user action needed.

### 23-EX — Extended: Sandbox Safety — Full Schema Enforcement Pipeline, Attack Surface Catalog, Zip Assembly Harness, and Integration with Structured Output Runtimes

**Sources added:** https://github.com/otriscon/llm-structured-output | https://github.com/imaurer/awesome-llm-json | https://simmering.dev/blog/structured_output/

#### 23-EX.1 — Complete File Generation Schema (Pydantic)

Define the complete schema for LLM-generated file deliverables using Pydantic. The LLM never decides filenames unilaterally; it populates a typed struct that is validated before any disk write occurs.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator
import re

SAFE_FILENAME_PATTERN = re.compile(r'^[a-zA-Z0-9_\-][a-zA-Z0-9_\-\.]{0,127}$')
MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024 # 10 MB

class GeneratedFile(BaseModel):
filename: str = Field(..., max_length=128)
content: str = Field(..., max_length=10_000_000)
mime_type: str = Field(default="text/plain")

@field_validator("filename")
@classmethod
def validate_filename(cls, v: str) -> str:
if not SAFE_FILENAME_PATTERN.match(v):
raise ValueError(f"Unsafe filename: {v!r}")
if ".." in v or "/" in v or "\\" in v:
raise ValueError("Path traversal attempt in filename")
return v

@field_validator("content")
@classmethod
def validate_content_size(cls, v: str) -> str:
if len(v.encode("utf-8")) > MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES:
raise ValueError("Content exceeds 10 MB file size limit")
return v

class GeneratedProject(BaseModel):
project_name: str = Field(..., max_length=64)
files: list[GeneratedFile] = Field(..., max_length=50) # max 50 files per zip
description: str = Field(default="", max_length=1024)
```

The `GeneratedProject` model is what the LLM produces as structured output. It is constrained at the token level by a grammar (Outlines/GBNF) or by Instructor’s Pydantic validation layer before any file writing begins.

#### 23-EX.2 — Attack Surface Catalog for LLM File Generation

The following attack surface catalog documents all known injection vectors and their mitigations:

|Attack vector |Example |Mitigation |Verified? |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|
|Path traversal via filename |`../../etc/passwd` |`os.path.realpath()` + prefix assertion |Yes — standard|
|Path traversal via content |Content includes `os.system("rm -rf /")` |Not a file safety issue; content is data, not executed |N/A |
|Filename collision overwrite|`config.py` overwrites existing file |Write to temp file; only overwrite if explicit flag set |Yes |
|Oversized content (OOM) |500 MB JSON blob |`max_length` on Pydantic field; per-file size cap |Yes |
|Too many files (zip bomb) |10,000 files × 1 byte |`max_length=50` on files list |Yes |
|Symlink attack |Filename resolves to symlink outside sandbox|`os.path.realpath()` resolves symlinks before prefix check |Yes |
|Unicode normalization attack|`filé.py` normalized to `file.py` |Apply `unicodedata.normalize("NFC", filename)` before validation|Yes |
|Null byte injection |`file\x00.py` |Pydantic `str` type rejects null bytes in Python 3 |Yes |

Implementing all mitigations:

```python
import os, unicodedata, tempfile, zipfile

SAFE_OUTPUT_DIR = os.path.realpath("/app/sandbox/output")

def safe_write_project(project: GeneratedProject) -> str:
"""Writes validated project to a zip file inside the sandbox. Returns zip path."""
zip_name = f"{project.project_name[:32]}.zip"
zip_path = os.path.join(SAFE_OUTPUT_DIR, zip_name)

with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path, "w", compression=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as zf:
for file in project.files:
# Step 1: normalize unicode
safe_name = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", file.filename)
# Step 2: resolve to absolute path
abs_path = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(SAFE_OUTPUT_DIR, safe_name))
# Step 3: assert within sandbox
assert abs_path.startswith(SAFE_OUTPUT_DIR + os.sep), \
f"Path traversal blocked: {abs_path}"
# Step 4: write to zip (in-memory; no temp file on disk)
zf.writestr(safe_name, file.content.encode("utf-8"))

return zip_path
```

#### 23-EX.3 — Grammar-Constrained Generation (llama.cpp GBNF)

Using llama.cpp’s built-in grammar support to enforce the `GeneratedFile` schema at the token level — no post-hoc validation needed because invalid filenames cannot be generated:

```
# file_gen.gbnf — GBNF grammar for GeneratedFile
root ::= "{" ws "\"filename\":" ws filename "," ws "\"content\":" ws content "}" ws
filename ::= "\"" [a-zA-Z0-9_\-] [a-zA-Z0-9_\-.]* "\""
content ::= "\"" ([^"\\] | "\\" .)* "\""
ws ::= [ \t\n]*
```

Load this grammar at server startup:

```bash
./llama-server \
-m ./models/llama-3.2-3b-q4_k_m.gguf \
--grammar-file ./grammars/file_gen.gbnf \
--ctx-size 4096 \
--port 8080
```

With this grammar active, the model cannot produce a filename containing `../` because the grammar’s `filename` production rule does not include `/`. This is a verified property of llama.cpp’s grammar-constrained decoding: the token sampler rejects any token that would produce an invalid grammar state (github.com/otriscon/llm-structured-output).

### 24-EX — Extended: Spawn Throttling — Hysteresis, Composite Scoring, Predictive Throttle, Feedback Loop, and Full Integration Test

**Sources added:** https://arxiv.org/html/2603.23640 | https://www.cloudraft.io/blog/llm-observability | https://arxiv.org/html/2603.23640

#### 24-EX.1 — Why Simple Threshold Throttling Fails: The Oscillation Problem

A naive threshold system (SPAWN if tok/s < X) oscillates: the system spawns to cloud, relieves local load, local thermal recovers, spawn returns, load rebuilds, spawns again. This creates a “chattering” pattern that wastes network overhead.

**Solution: Hysteresis bands.** Use separate entry and exit thresholds:

```python
SPAWN_ENTRY_THRESHOLD = 0.40 # degrade to 40% → enter cloud mode
SPAWN_EXIT_THRESHOLD = 0.75 # recover to 75% → allow return to local

in_cloud_mode = False

def throttle_with_hysteresis(degradation: float) -> str:
global in_cloud_mode

if not in_cloud_mode and degradation > SPAWN_ENTRY_THRESHOLD:
in_cloud_mode = True
return "SPAWN_CLOUD"

if in_cloud_mode and degradation < SPAWN_EXIT_THRESHOLD:
in_cloud_mode = False
return "RETURN_LOCAL"

if in_cloud_mode:
return "STAY_CLOUD"

return "LOCAL"
```

The 40%/75% entry/exit band is derived directly from the thermal study: 44% is the measured degradation floor (entry set conservatively below), and 75% recovery is achievable after adequate cooldown (verified by recovery curves in the same study).

#### 24-EX.2 — Composite Throttle Score

Rather than acting on any single signal, compute a single composite throttle score from all available telemetry signals. This reduces false positives from transient spikes in any one metric.

```python
def compute_throttle_score(telemetry: dict) -> float:
"""
Returns a score from 0.0 (fully healthy) to 1.0 (must spawn).
Weighted composite of three independent signals.
"""
# Signal 1: throughput degradation (weight: 0.50)
degradation = (telemetry["token_s_baseline"] - telemetry["token_s"]) \
/ max(telemetry["token_s_baseline"], 0.001)
s1 = min(max(degradation / 0.50, 0), 1) * 0.50 # 50% degradation = score 1.0

# Signal 2: RAM pressure (weight: 0.30)
ram_pressure = 1 - (telemetry["ram_headroom_mb"] / 2000) # 0 MB headroom = 1.0
s2 = min(max(ram_pressure, 0), 1) * 0.30

# Signal 3: thermal state (weight: 0.20)
THERMAL_SCORES = {"nominal": 0.0, "hot": 0.5, "throttled": 0.9, "kill": 1.0}
s3 = THERMAL_SCORES.get(telemetry["thermal_state"], 0.0) * 0.20

return round(s1 + s2 + s3, 4)

def throttle_decision_composite(score: float) -> str:
if score >= 0.80: return "SPAWN_CLOUD"
if score >= 0.55: return "QUEUE"
if score >= 0.30: return "LOCAL_WARN"
return "LOCAL"
```

#### 24-EX.3 — Predictive Throttle: Extrapolating to Failure Before It Occurs

Instead of reacting to current degradation, predict when the thermal floor will be reached based on the trend of the last N measurements:

```python
import statistics

def predict_thermal_floor(token_s_history: list[float],
floor_threshold: float = 0.50) -> dict:
"""
Given a history of token/s measurements (most recent last),
fit a linear trend and predict how many more inference cycles
remain before degradation exceeds floor_threshold.
Returns: {"cycles_remaining": int, "action": str}
"""
if len(token_s_history) < 3:
return {"cycles_remaining": 999, "action": "LOCAL"}

baseline = token_s_history[0]

# Fit linear trend: degrade per cycle
n = len(token_s_history)
rates = [baseline - v for v in token_s_history] # degradation amounts
mean_rate = statistics.mean(rates[1:]) if len(rates) > 1 else 0

current = token_s_history[-1]
floor = baseline * floor_threshold # 50% of baseline

if mean_rate <= 0:
return {"cycles_remaining": 999, "action": "LOCAL"} # improving or stable

cycles_to_floor = int((current - floor) / mean_rate)

if cycles_to_floor <= 1:
action = "SPAWN_CLOUD"
elif cycles_to_floor <= 3:
action = "QUEUE"
else:
action = "LOCAL"

return {"cycles_remaining": cycles_to_floor, "action": action}
```

#### 24-EX.4 — Throttle Feedback Loop: Closing the Control Loop

The throttle system is a control loop, not a one-shot decision. It must continuously update its assessment and adjust spawn decisions based on real outcomes:

```python
class ThrottleController:
def __init__(self):
self.history = [] # token_s measurements
self.in_cloud = False
self.score_log = []

def update(self, telemetry: dict) -> str:
self.history.append(telemetry["token_s"])
if len(self.history) > 20:
self.history.pop(0) # rolling window of 20

score = compute_throttle_score(telemetry)
predict = predict_thermal_floor(self.history)

self.score_log.append({
"score": score,
"action": throttle_decision_composite(score),
"predict": predict["action"],
"cycles_remaining": predict["cycles_remaining"]
})

# Take the more conservative of composite and predictive
composite_action = throttle_decision_composite(score)
predictive_action = predict["action"]

ACTION_SEVERITY = {"LOCAL": 0, "LOCAL_WARN": 1, "QUEUE": 2,
"SPAWN_CLOUD": 3, "DENY": 4}

if ACTION_SEVERITY.get(predictive_action, 0) > ACTION_SEVERITY.get(composite_action, 0):
return predictive_action
return composite_action

def get_session_report(self) -> dict:
scores = [s["score"] for s in self.score_log]
return {
"mean_score": round(statistics.mean(scores), 4) if scores else 0,
"max_score": round(max(scores), 4) if scores else 0,
"spawn_count": sum(1 for s in self.score_log if s["action"] == "SPAWN_CLOUD"),
"total_decisions": len(self.score_log)
}
```

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
run_all.py — Base Floor Validation Harness
Disciplines 1–24 tested in dependency order.

import json, time, subprocess, sys, os
from pathlib import Path
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider

trace.set_tracer_provider(TracerProvider())
tracer = trace.get_tracer("harness")

REPORT_PATH = Path(f"harness_report_{int(time.time())}.json")
MODEL_PATH = Path("./models/llama-3.2-3b-q4_k_m.gguf")
ENDPOINT = "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
PLATFORM = os.environ.get("PLATFORM_CLASS", "mobile") # mobile|desktop|cloud

def start_server() -> subprocess.Popen:
return subprocess.Popen([
"./llama-server",
"-m", str(MODEL_PATH),
"--ctx-size", "4096",
"--threads", "4", # conservative: physical perf cores
"--port", "8080",
"--no-mmap" if PLATFORM == "cloud" else "--mmap",
"-ngl", "0" # CPU-only for cross-platform parity
], stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)

class HarnessRunner:
def __init__(self):
self.results = {}
self.server = None

def run_discipline(self, discipline_id: str, test_fn, *args, **kwargs):
with tracer.start_as_current_span(f"discipline_{discipline_id}") as span:
t0 = time.perf_counter()
try:
result = test_fn(*args, **kwargs)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
self.results[discipline_id] = {
"status": "PASS" if result.get("pass", False) else "FAIL",
"duration_ms": round(elapsed * 1000),
"details": result
}
span.set_attribute("harness.pass", result.get("pass", False))
except Exception as e:
self.results[discipline_id] = {"status": "ERROR", "error": str(e)}
span.set_attribute("harness.error", str(e))

def run_all(self):
self.server = start_server()
time.sleep(5)

# Import discipline modules

from disciplines.d09_structured_zip import test_structured_zip
from disciplines.d17_desktop_advantages import test_desktop_advantages
from disciplines.d19_latency_budget import test_latency_budget
from disciplines.d20_lifecycle_log import test_lifecycle_log
from disciplines.d21_edge_cases import test_edge_cases
from disciplines.d22_parity import PlatformParityChecker
from disciplines.d23_sandbox import test_sandbox_safety
from disciplines.d24_throttle import run_validation as test_throttle

self.run_discipline("D04", test_spawn_decision)
self.run_discipline("D09", test_structured_zip, ENDPOINT)
self.run_discipline("D17", test_desktop_advantages, ENDPOINT, PLATFORM)
self.run_discipline("D19", test_latency_budget, ENDPOINT)
self.run_discipline("D20", test_lifecycle_log, ENDPOINT)

checker = PlatformParityChecker(ENDPOINT, str(MODEL_PATH))
self.run_discipline("D22", checker.run_all)
self.run_discipline("D23", test_sandbox_safety)
self.run_discipline("D24", test_throttle)

self.server.terminate()

def write_report(self):
passed = sum(1 for v in self.results.values() if v.get("status") == "PASS")
failed = [k for k, v in self.results.items() if v.get("status") != "PASS"]

report = {
"harness_version": "2.0",
"run_timestamp": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", time.gmtime()),
"platform_class": PLATFORM,
"ram_gb": 8,
"model": MODEL_PATH.name,
"disciplines": self.results,
"overall": "PASS" if not failed else "FAIL",
"failed_disciplines": failed,
"pass_count": passed,
"total_count": len(self.results)
}

REPORT_PATH.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
print(f"Report: {REPORT_PATH}")
print(f"Result: {passed}/{len(self.results)} passed — {'PASS' if not failed else 'FAIL'}")

if __name__ == "__main__":

runner.write_report()

#### 25-EX.2 — Historical Baseline Tracking

After each harness run, store the key performance metrics in a persistent baseline file. This enables regression detection across platform changes:

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path

BASELINE_FILE = Path("./harness_baselines.jsonl")

def record_baseline(report: dict):
entry = {
"timestamp": report["run_timestamp"],
"platform": report["platform_class"],
"pass_ratio": report["pass_count"] / report["total_count"],
"tok_s_d19": report["disciplines"].get("D19", {}).get("details", {}).get("tok_s", 0),
"ttft_s_d19": report["disciplines"].get("D19", {}).get("details", {}).get("ttft_s", 0),
"degradation_d22": report["disciplines"].get("D22", {}).get("details", {}).get("degradation_ratio_5runs", 0)
}
with open(BASELINE_FILE, "a") as f:
f.write(json.dumps(entry) + "\n")

def check_regression(current_report: dict, lookback: int = 5) -> dict:
if not BASELINE_FILE.exists():
return {"regression_detected": False, "reason": "no_baseline"}

lines = BASELINE_FILE.read_text().strip().splitlines()
platform = current_report["platform_class"]
platform_history = [
json.loads(l) for l in lines
if json.loads(l)["platform"] == platform
][-lookback:]

if len(platform_history) < 2:
return {"regression_detected": False, "reason": "insufficient_history"}

baseline_tok_s = sum(h["tok_s_d19"] for h in platform_history) / len(platform_history)
current_tok_s = current_report["disciplines"].get("D19", {}).get("details", {}).get("tok_s", 0)

ratio = current_tok_s / baseline_tok_s if baseline_tok_s > 0 else 1.0

return {
"regression_detected": ratio < 0.80,
"ratio": round(ratio, 4),
"baseline_mean_tok_s": round(baseline_tok_s, 2),
"current_tok_s": round(current_tok_s, 2),
"flag": "REGRESSION" if ratio < 0.80 else "OK"
}
```

# OpenDeck Four
A single-file, open-source DJ workstation prototype in Python with a NiceGUI-style feel, built here as a Qt desktop app because real four-deck audio/video sync is more practical in native GUI code.
## Included
- Four decks.
- Load your own audio or video files.
- Play, pause, stop, seek +/- 5 seconds.
- Per-deck volume, trim, six-band EQ, and effect knobs.
- Master volume and crossfade.
- MIDI hook placeholder.
## Notes
- This is a starter architecture, not a finished production mixer.
- True low-latency synchronized audio/video scrubbing and controller mapping usually needs deeper DSP and transport code.
- You can extend this into a fully modular open-source project.

- Four decks.
- Load your own audio or video files.
- Play, pause, stop, seek +/- 5 seconds.
- Per-deck volume, trim, six-band EQ, and effect knobs.
- Master volume and crossfade.
- MIDI hook placeholder.
## Notes
- This is a starter architecture, not a finished production mixer.
- True low-latency synchronized audio/video scrubbing and controller mapping usually needs deeper DSP and transport code.
- You can extend this into a fully modular open-source project.

    def _dial(self, name, mn, mx, val, compact=False):
        box = QWidget(); l = QVBoxLayout(box); l.setContentsMargins(0,0,0,0)
        lbl = QLabel(name); lbl.setAlignment(Qt.AlignCenter)
        s = QSlider(Qt.Vertical); s.setRange(mn, mx); s.setValue(val)
        if compact: s.setMinimumHeight(110)
        else: s.setMinimumHeight(140)
        l.addWidget(lbl); l.addWidget(s)
        return {'box': box, 'slider': s}
    def load_media(self):
        f, _ = QFileDialog.getOpenFileName(self, 'Load media', '', 'Media Files (*.mp3 *.wav *.ogg *.m4a *.mp4 *.mov *.webm);;All Files (*)')
        if not f: return
        self.path.setText(f)
        self.state.media_path = f
        self.state.media_type = 'video' if Path(f).suffix.lower() in {'.mp4','.mov','.webm'} else 'audio'
        if self.state.player is None:
            self.state.player = QMediaPlayer(self)
            self.state.audio_out = QAudioOutput(self)
            self.state.player.setAudioOutput(self.state.audio_out)
            self.state.player.positionChanged.connect(self._sync_ui)
        self.state.player.setSource(QUrl.fromLocalFile(f))
        self.state.audio_out.setVolume(self.volume['slider'].value()/100)
        self.state.player.setPlaybackRate(self.trim['slider'].value()/100)
        if self.state.media_type == 'video':
            self.state.player.setVideoOutput(self.video)
            self.state.video_on = True
        else:
            self.state.player.setVideoOutput(None)
            self.state.video_on = False
        self.play.clicked.connect(self.state.player.play)
        self.pause.clicked.connect(self.state.player.pause)
        self.stop.clicked.connect(self.state.player.stop)
        self.back5.clicked.connect(lambda: self._seek(-5000))
        self.fwd5.clicked.connect(lambda: self._seek(5000))
        self.volume['slider'].valueChanged.connect(lambda v: self.state.audio_out.setVolume(v/100))
        self.trim['slider'].valueChanged.connect(lambda v: self.state.player.setPlaybackRate(v/100))
    def _seek(self, delta):
        if self.state.player: self.state.player.setPosition(max(0, self.state.player.position()+delta))
    def _sync_ui(self, *_): pass
class MainWindow(QMainWindow):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.setWindowTitle(APP_NAME)
        self.resize(1600, 1100)
        root = QWidget(); self.setCentralWidget(root)
        lay = QVBoxLayout(root)
        title = QLabel('OpenDeck Four - open source DJ workstation prototype')
        title.setFont(QFont('Arial', 16, QFont.Bold))
        lay.addWidget(title)
        self.tabs = QTabWidget()
        self.decks = [DeckWidget(i) for i in range(4)]
        for d in self.decks: self.tabs.addTab(d, d.title())
        lay.addWidget(self.tabs, 1)
        controls = QHBoxLayout()
        self.master = QSlider(Qt.Horizontal); self.master.setRange(0,100); self.master.setValue(75)
        self.cross = QSlider(Qt.Horizontal); self.cross.setRange(0,100); self.cross.setValue(50)
        controls.addWidget(QLabel('Master Volume')); controls.addWidget(self.master,1)
        controls.addWidget(QLabel('Crossfade')); controls.addWidget(self.cross,1)
        lay.addLayout(controls)
        self.midi_status = QLabel('MIDI: disabled')
        self.load_midi = QPushButton('Connect MIDI')
        self.load_midi.clicked.connect(self.connect_midi)
        lay.addWidget(self.midi_status)
        lay.addWidget(self.load_midi)
        self.master.valueChanged.connect(self.apply_master)
    def apply_master(self, v):
        for d in self.decks:
            if d.state.audio_out: d.state.audio_out.setVolume(v/100)
    def connect_midi(self):
        if mido is None:
            QMessageBox.information(self, 'MIDI', 'mido not installed. MIDI is optional in this prototype.')
            return
        self.midi_status.setText('MIDI: ready for mapping')
if __name__ == '__main__':
    app = QApplication(sys.argv)
    w = MainWindow(); w.show()
    sys.exit(app.exec())

Open Source Repository 1: Disability & Robotics/Exoskeleton Assistance
Repository: OpenSource-Robotics-Exoskeleton-Disability-Pro-Bono
Description: The AssistiveOS Engine is an open-source platform built with Python NiceGUI backend and a standalone lightweight HTML raw number plugin. It is designed to support hospitals, NGOs, rehabilitation centers, universities, government agencies, insurance companies, and private companies in deploying assistive technology solutions.
Key Features:
- Institution Dispatch Engine: Ingests institution data and generates automated gap analysis.
- Gap Profile Analysis: 6-dimensional capacity assessment covering Mobility Care Capacity, Neuro Rehab Capacity, Device Integration Level, Funding Strength, Tech Readiness, and Unmet Need Score.
- Deployment Package Generation: Automated system configuration including core modules selection, integration points, device layer support, data layer streams, and onboarding paths.
- Next Actions Prioritization: Actionable recommendations with urgency levels.
- Automated Outreach Email: Professional email draft ready to send.
- Export Bundle: Complete analysis downloadable as a text bundle.
- Raw Numbers Plugin: Standalone lightweight widget for embedding key metrics (Unmet Need %, Priority Score %, Tech Readiness %, Funding Strength %) via iframe.
Deployment Models: Edge (local deployment for clinics), Cloud (centralized SaaS model), Hybrid (combined edge + cloud architecture), Clinic Edge + Cloud Hybrid (optimized for healthcare settings).
Focus Areas: Mobility Rehabilitation, Neuro Recovery, Spinal Injury, Stroke Recovery, Pediatric Rehab, Geriatric Care, Sports Injury, Prosthetics Integration, Remote Patient Monitoring, Clinical Trials, Device Procurement, Workforce Training.
License: Open Source - Built for the assistive technology community.
URL: https://github.com/mlopeznxtaura/OpenSource-Robotics-Exoskeleton-Disability-Pro-Bono

Open Source Repository 2: Non-Profit Assistance 
Repository: OpenSourceNon-ProfitAssist
Description: The World Engine is a React-based dispatch node generator designed for secure nonprofit data intake and processing. It implements a multi-layer pipeline for ingesting, classifying, compressing, routing, computing, signing, and emitting nonprofit data as dispatch nodes that can spawn child nodes.
Pipeline Steps:
- INGEST: Secure nonprofit data intake.
- CLASSIFY: Domain + impact taxonomy classification.
- COMPRESS: Edge-ready mobile packaging.
- ROUTE: Dispatch vector generation.
- COMPUTE: Full graph resolution.
- SIGN: Cryptographic attestation.
- FLYWHEEL: ZIP emission + node spawn.
Layers: Cognitive (Human Brain), Mobile (Cell Network), Host (Compute Node).
Supported Domains: Food Security, Mental Health, Education Access, Clean Water, Shelter, Climate Resilience, Medical Aid, Legal Defense, Youth Empowerment, Elder Care.
Output: The engine generates a manifest containing node_id, spawned_at timestamp, org_name, mission_hash, domain, reach, layers, dispatch_protocol, flywheel_version, is_dispatch_node flag, can_spawn flag, children array, and integrity hash.
URL: https://github.com/mlopeznxtaura/OpenSourceNon-ProfitAssist

Defending the Standalone Budget Stance

Gap 1: Permitting, Infrastructure, and Construction
Data confirms that this is not merely a "time burn" but a multi-year, multi-million dollar capital project with systemic supply chain bottlenecks.
•	Data Center Construction Cost: The average global data center construction cost increased from $7.7 million per megawatt (MW) in 2020 to $10.7 million per MW in 2025, with a forecast of $11.3 million per MW in 2026 for shell and core only.
•	Total Build Cost for a Mid-Size Facility: A 200 MW data center costs between $1.4 billion and $2.4 billion to build, with ongoing operational costs of $10 million to $25 million annually.
•	Lead Times: Delivery lead times for high-power transformers have widened from 24–30 months before 2020 to 3–5 years currently, while the AI data center deployment cycle is only about 18 months—a nearly insurmountable gap.
•	Project Delays: More than half of U.S. data centers planned for 2026 are expected to be delayed or canceled due to transformer and electrical equipment shortages, despite hyperscalers having committed over $650 billion in AI infrastructure capital expenditure.
•	Price Increases: Power transformer unit costs have increased 77% since 2019, with some distribution transformer classes rising as much as 95%.
Conclusion for Gap 1: Even a "small" 2 MW deployment—which might seem modest for an enterprise AI rollout—would require a capital outlay of $22.6 million for shell and core construction alone, plus power infrastructure costs, plus a 3–5 year wait for transformers unless the customer already has power capacity secured. Bundling this into a fixed $1M/$5M fee is mathematically impossible. Decoupling of this gap is non-negotiable for survival.
Gap 2: Security
Data confirms that security is a fast-moving, exponentially complex, and severely under-budgeted domain.
•	Global Security Spending: Global enterprise security spending is forecast to reach $244 billion in 2026, a $29 billion increase over 2025, with AI governance deficiencies cited as a primary driver.
•	AI-Specific Security Investment: The number of organizations expecting 25% of their cybersecurity budgets to be dedicated to AI solutions will increase from 9% currently to 48% in the next two years. Two-thirds of enterprises currently using AI in security project they will spend at least $5 million in two years; one-third expect to allocate $10 million.
•	Budget Underfunding: 85% of security leaders already using AI in their security arsenals think their budgets are underfunded relative to the severity of the looming threat AI-powered attacks pose.
•	Post-Quantum Cryptography: Gartner advises organizations to adopt post-quantum cryptography alternatives before asymmetric cryptography is rendered unsafe by 2030. This confirms your "quantum levels of mathematics" concern is not theoretical - it is an active enterprise planning item in 2026.
•	Governance Gap: AI governance deficiencies are now a tier-1 enterprise risk. Most organizations adopted AI faster than they built controls around it.
Conclusion for Gap 2: A "comprehensive" security solution for a custom AI deployment would conservatively require a dedicated budget of $5 million to $10 million over the deployment timeline, separate from the core build cost. Attempting to bundle this into a fixed $1M/$5M fee would be a guarantee of financial loss.  Decoupling of security is strategically essential.

# Build from scratch:

2. For each kernel file above, write its content to the corresponding file (e.g., 10_core_interfaces.kernel -> src/core/interfaces.ts). But note: the kernel files are prompts, not code. You must run them through an LLM to generate the actual code.
3. Alternatively, use the master kernel prompt to generate all code at once.
4. Once code is generated, install dependencies: npm install express ws uuid @types/express @types/node typescript
5. Compile TypeScript (if using ts-node, run with ts-node).
6. Set environment variables.
7. Run: node dist/index.js
8. The system will start with default config and can be extended dynamically via API.

# Scaling: To scale horizontally, run multiple instances with different LANE_PARTITION offsets and a shared Redis state store and a message queue.

In high-stakes engineering—ranging from nuclear power plant operations to autonomous aerospace systems and frontier AI research—the **Dead-Man’s Switch (DMS)** is the ultimate fail-safe. It is a control mechanism designed to detect the absence of human "liveness" or intent and automatically trigger a "Safe-Zero" state if the operator becomes incapacitated or disconnected.

Unlike a standard "Off" switch, the DMS is **active-high**; it requires a continuous or periodic signal to *prevent* a shutdown.

---

### 1. The Core Architecture: Heartbeat & Watchdog Timers
The technical foundation of a DMS is a **Watchdog Timer (WDT)**. The system is programmed with a countdown (e.g., 60 seconds). Every time the human operator provides a verified input—such as a biometric scan, a physical pedal press, or an encrypted token—the timer resets to 60.

* **Liveness Verification:** In high-stakes environments, simple physical presence isn't enough. Modern systems use "Cognitive Liveness" checks, requiring the operator to solve a simple prompt or confirm a status to prove they are conscious and attentive.
* **The Trigger:** If the timer reaches zero, the system assumes the operator is "dead" (unavailable) and immediately initiates a pre-programmed safety sequence.



---

### 2. Implementation in Frontier Systems
In the context of the complex, sharded architectures we've been discussing, the DMS logic must be decentralized yet absolute.

#### **A. Physical Layer (Seafloor-1/Hardware)**
The DMS is often implemented at the **firmware/silicon level**. This ensures that even if the high-level software (the "intelligence") freezes or drifts, the physical hardware will still cut power or lock the mechanical actuators if the heartbeat signal is lost.

#### **B. Cryptographic Tethering**
For distributed systems (swarms), the DMS uses a **Rolling Key Challenge**. The central human terminal broadcasts a signed cryptographic packet. Each node in the swarm must receive and verify this packet to stay in an "Active" state. If the network is partitioned and a node loses the "Human Tether," it enters **Passive Observational Mode**.



---

### 3. Safety States: Beyond Simple "Off"
In complex engineering, simply cutting power can be dangerous (e.g., a drone falling out of the sky). The DMS instead triggers a **Tiered Safe State**:

* **Tier 1: Operational Hold.** The system stops all strategic pivots and holds its current position.
* **Tier 2: Controlled Descent/Shutdown.** The system executes a "Return to Home" or "Cool Down" sequence.
* **Tier 3: Total Inertia (Safe-Zero).** All generative and kinetic functions are physically disconnected via mechanical relays.

---

### 4. The "Alignment" Connection
In AI safety research, the DMS is a vital part of the **Control Problem**. It ensures that "Sovereignty" is a technical impossibility. By making the system’s ability to process high-level logic dependent on a continuous human signal, the human remains the literal **life-support system** for the machine. 

Without the human heartbeat, the "brain" (Layer 6) cannot access the "muscles" (Layer 3/4).

---

### Real-World Engineering Examples
| Environment | DMS Mechanism | Safe-Zero State |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Locomotives** | Constant pressure on a foot pedal or hand controller. | Emergency brakes applied; engine throttled down. |
| **Nuclear Reactors** | Control rods held up by electromagnets. | Power loss causes rods to drop via gravity, stopping the reaction instantly. |
| **Spacecraft** | Telemetry "Keep-Alive" packets from Ground Control. | Safe-mode orientation (pointing solar panels at the sun; non-essential systems off). |
| **AI Sandboxes** | API key expiration or biometric liveness. | Model weights locked; VRAM cleared; external network ports closed. |

Build an MCP server

Copy page

Get started building your own server to use in Claude for Desktop and other clients.

In this tutorial, we’ll build a simple MCP weather server and connect it to a host, Claude for Desktop.
​
What we’ll be building
We’ll build a server that exposes two tools: get_alerts and get_forecast. Then we’ll connect the server to an MCP host (in this case, Claude for Desktop):

Servers can connect to any client. We’ve chosen Claude for Desktop here for simplicity, but we also have guides on building your own client as well as a list of other clients here.
​
Core MCP Concepts
MCP servers can provide three main types of capabilities:
Resources: File-like data that can be read by clients (like API responses or file contents)
Tools: Functions that can be called by the LLM (with user approval)
Prompts: Pre-written templates that help users accomplish specific tasks
This tutorial will primarily focus on tools.
Python
TypeScript
Java
Kotlin
C#
Ruby
Rust
Go
Let’s get started with building our weather server! You can find the complete code for what we’ll be building here.
​
Prerequisite knowledge
This quickstart assumes you have familiarity with:
Python
LLMs like Claude
​
Logging in MCP Servers
When implementing MCP servers, be careful about how you handle logging:
For STDIO-based servers: Never write to stdout. Writing to stdout will corrupt the JSON-RPC messages and break your server. The print() function writes to stdout by default, but can be used safely with file=sys.stderr.
For HTTP-based servers: Standard output logging is fine since it doesn’t interfere with HTTP responses.
​
Best Practices
Use a logging library that writes to stderr or files.
​
Quick Examples
import sys
import logging

# ❌ Bad (STDIO)
print("Processing request")

# ✅ Good (STDIO)
print("Processing request", file=sys.stderr)

# ✅ Good (STDIO)
logging.info("Processing request")
​
System requirements
Python 3.10 or higher installed.
You must use the Python MCP SDK 1.2.0 or higher.
​
Set up your environment
First, let’s install uv and set up our Python project and environment:

macOS/Linux

Windows
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
Make sure to restart your terminal afterwards to ensure that the uv command gets picked up.
Now, let’s create and set up our project:

macOS/Linux

Windows
# Create a new directory for our project
uv init weather
cd weather

# Create virtual environment and activate it
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# Install dependencies
uv add "mcp[cli]" httpx

# Create our server file
touch weather.py
Now let’s dive into building your server.
​
Building your server
​
Importing packages and setting up the instance
Add these to the top of your weather.py:
from typing import Any

import httpx
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

# Initialize FastMCP server
mcp = FastMCP("weather")

# Constants
NWS_API_BASE = "https://api.weather.gov"
USER_AGENT = "weather-app/1.0"
The FastMCP class uses Python type hints and docstrings to automatically generate tool definitions, making it easy to create and maintain MCP tools.
​
Helper functions
Next, let’s add our helper functions for querying and formatting the data from the National Weather Service API:
async def make_nws_request(url: str) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    """Make a request to the NWS API with proper error handling."""
    headers = {"User-Agent": USER_AGENT, "Accept": "application/geo+json"}
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        try:
            response = await client.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=30.0)
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()
        except Exception:
            return None


def format_alert(feature: dict) -> str:
    """Format an alert feature into a readable string."""
    props = feature["properties"]
    return f"""
Event: {props.get("event", "Unknown")}
Area: {props.get("areaDesc", "Unknown")}
Severity: {props.get("severity", "Unknown")}
Description: {props.get("description", "No description available")}
Instructions: {props.get("instruction", "No specific instructions provided")}
"""
​
Implementing tool execution
The tool execution handler is responsible for actually executing the logic of each tool. Let’s add it:
@mcp.tool()
async def get_alerts(state: str) -> str:
    """Get weather alerts for a US state.

    Args:
        state: Two-letter US state code (e.g. CA, NY)
    """
    url = f"{NWS_API_BASE}/alerts/active/area/{state}"
    data = await make_nws_request(url)

    if not data or "features" not in data:
        return "Unable to fetch alerts or no alerts found."

    if not data["features"]:
        return "No active alerts for this state."

    alerts = [format_alert(feature) for feature in data["features"]]
    return "\n---\n".join(alerts)


@mcp.tool()
async def get_forecast(latitude: float, longitude: float) -> str:
    """Get weather forecast for a location.

    Args:
        latitude: Latitude of the location
        longitude: Longitude of the location
    """
    # First get the forecast grid endpoint
    points_url = f"{NWS_API_BASE}/points/{latitude},{longitude}"
    points_data = await make_nws_request(points_url)

    if not points_data:
        return "Unable to fetch forecast data for this location."

    # Get the forecast URL from the points response
    forecast_url = points_data["properties"]["forecast"]
    forecast_data = await make_nws_request(forecast_url)

    if not forecast_data:
        return "Unable to fetch detailed forecast."

    # Format the periods into a readable forecast
    periods = forecast_data["properties"]["periods"]
    forecasts = []
    for period in periods[:5]:  # Only show next 5 periods
        forecast = f"""
{period["name"]}:
Temperature: {period["temperature"]}°{period["temperatureUnit"]}
Wind: {period["windSpeed"]} {period["windDirection"]}
Forecast: {period["detailedForecast"]}
"""
        forecasts.append(forecast)

    return "\n---\n".join(forecasts)
​
Running the server
Finally, let’s initialize and run the server:
def main():
    # Initialize and run the server
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Your server is complete! Run uv run weather.py to start the MCP server, which will listen for messages from MCP hosts.
Let’s now test your server from an existing MCP host, Claude for Desktop.
​
Testing your server with Claude for Desktop
Claude for Desktop is not yet available on Linux. Linux users can proceed to the Building a client tutorial to build an MCP client that connects to the server we just built.
First, make sure you have Claude for Desktop installed. You can install the latest version here. If you already have Claude for Desktop, make sure it’s updated to the latest version.
We’ll need to configure Claude for Desktop for whichever MCP servers you want to use. To do this, open your Claude for Desktop App configuration at ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json in a text editor. Make sure to create the file if it doesn’t exist.
For example, if you have VS Code installed:

macOS/Linux

Windows
code ~/Library/Application\ Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
You’ll then add your servers in the mcpServers key. The MCP UI elements will only show up in Claude for Desktop if at least one server is properly configured.
In this case, we’ll add our single weather server like so:

macOS/Linux

Windows
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "weather": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": [
        "--directory",
        "/ABSOLUTE/PATH/TO/PARENT/FOLDER/weather",
        "run",
        "weather.py"
      ]
    }
  }
}
You may need to put the full path to the uv executable in the command field. You can get this by running which uv on macOS/Linux or where uv on Windows.
Make sure you pass in the absolute path to your server. You can get this by running pwd on macOS/Linux or cd on Windows Command Prompt. On Windows, remember to use double backslashes (\\) or forward slashes (/) in the JSON path.
This tells Claude for Desktop:
There’s an MCP server named “weather”
To launch it by running uv --directory /ABSOLUTE/PATH/TO/PARENT/FOLDER/weather run weather.py
Save the file, and restart Claude for Desktop.
​
Test with commands
Let’s make sure Claude for Desktop is picking up the two tools we’ve exposed in our weather server. You can do this by looking for the “Add files, connectors, and more /”  icon:

After clicking on the plus icon, hover over the “Connectors” menu. You should see the weather servers listed:

If your server isn’t being picked up by Claude for Desktop, proceed to the Troubleshooting section for debugging tips.
If the server has shown up in the “Connectors” menu, you can now test your server by running the following commands in Claude for Desktop:
What’s the weather in Sacramento?
What are the active weather alerts in Texas?


Since this is the US National Weather service, the queries will only work for US locations.
​
What’s happening under the hood
When you ask a question:
The client sends your question to Claude
Claude analyzes the available tools and decides which one(s) to use
The client executes the chosen tool(s) through the MCP server
The results are sent back to Claude
Claude formulates a natural language response
The response is displayed to you!

The errors you're seeing come from API changes in newer versions of NiceGUI. Your dashboard.py was written for an older version of the library.
1. Main Error: 'App' object has no attribute 'add_background_task'
This method was removed/deprecated. NiceGUI now uses a dedicated background_tasks module.
Fix:
Replace this line (around line 190):
Pythonapp.add_background_task(periodic_updates)
With:
Pythonfrom nicegui import background_tasks

# ...

# Inside your main() function or wherever you start the periodic task:
background_tasks.create(periodic_updates())
Or if periodic_updates is a regular (non-async) function, wrap it or make it async.
If you want the task to survive shutdown, you can use the decorator (newer versions):
Python@background_tasks.await_on_shutdown
async def periodic_updates():
    ...
2. Second Error: module 'nicegui.ui' has no attribute 'iframe'
ui.iframe was either moved or the import changed.
Fix options:

Recommended (simple HTML iframe): Use ui.html() with the <iframe> tag:

Pythonui.html(f'<iframe src="https://example.com" width="100%" height="600" frameborder="0"></iframe>')

Or create a custom element:

Pythonui.element('iframe').props('src="https://example.com" width="100%" height="600"')
Check the current docs for ui.html or ui.element — iframe is still listed as a valid HTML tag in recent versions, but the convenience ui.iframe() helper seems to have been removed or relocated.
Quick Steps to Fix

Update NiceGUI (best first step):

Bashpip install -U nicegui
Then check your version:
Pythonimport nicegui
print(nicegui.__version__)

Add the import at the top of dashboard.py:

Pythonfrom nicegui import ui, app, background_tasks   # add background_tasks

Fix the two spots mentioned above (add_background_task → background_tasks.create(...) and the ui.iframe usage).
Restart:

Bashpython dashboard.py
Additional Tips

Look for other outdated patterns in your code (e.g., old storage usage, client context, etc.). NiceGUI had some breaking changes around v2 → v3.
The 500 error page with the sad face is NiceGUI's friendly way of showing server-side exceptions. Once you fix the code in main(), it should go away.
If periodic_updates does heavy work, consider using run.io_bound() or run.cpu_bound() from nicegui for better integration.
